headline: Google's new Genie 4 AI generates 2-minute interactive worlds with audio and real-time updates
summary: Google's Genie 4 world model now creates more realistic, interactive experiences up to two minutes long, complete with generated audio and real-time natural language updates. It's powered by Gemini 3.8 Flash.
details: Google has officially unveiled Genie 4, its latest world model designed to generate interactive AI experiences. This new iteration boasts significant updates, including more realistic worlds, the ability to update experiences in real-time via natural language prompts, and the generation of accompanying audio. It can create experiences up to two minutes long, doubling the previous Genie 3 model's one-minute limit.

Under the hood, Genie 4 leverages Gemini 3.8 Flash to enhance its simulations, contributing to the model's improved capabilities. Google envisions Genie 4 as a versatile tool, potentially aiding filmmakers in pre-visualization, game developers in prototyping new ideas, and facilitating training scenarios for robots.

However, Google notes a current limitation: as simulations extend in duration, details and object permanence within the generated worlds can sometimes shift. This is a known challenge in long-form AI generation that the company is addressing.

Genie 4 is currently launching as a "research preview" for "trusted testers." Google has stated it will be "coming soon" to Google AI Ultra subscribers and has opened a waitlist for those interested in trying it within Project Genie.

headline_marked: [[Anthropic illegally trained Claude]] with Stanford professors' books, judge rules
headline: Anthropic illegally trained Claude with Stanford professors' books, judge rules
summary: A federal judge ruled against Anthropic for illegal scraping, but also justified the legal acquisition of books for AI training as fair use. This led to a $1.5 billion settlement, though some authors are seeking more.
details: A federal judge ruled in May 2026 that AI giant Anthropic illegally scraped and pirated the work of over 10 Stanford professors to train its Claude models. This ruling came as part of a lawsuit addressing the use of copyrighted material in AI training.

However, the judge also justified the legal acquisition of books to train Claude’s Large Language Models (LLMs) as fair use. He compared AI training to how humans can read, internalize, and remember a book’s themes and style without replicating it directly.

A $1.5 billion settlement was reached, covering authors and publishers of nearly 500,000 registered works. Despite this, some authors, including professor emeritus of English Wolff, believe the settlement is insufficient.

Wolff, whose 10 publications were used without permission, described the uncompensated use of his work as a "form of slave labor." He argues that the settlement still grants Anthropic too much freedom to use literature for profit without proper remuneration.

Wolff, alongside English professor Chang-rae Lee, opted out of the Bartz settlement. They filed a separate non-class lawsuit, Cruz v. Anthropic, seeking a jury trial for full statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work, significantly more than the Bartz settlement's approximate $3,000 per work.

If successful, Wolff and his fellow authors aim to secure a permanent injunction against Claude model training using their specific works. This would prevent future unauthorized use of their intellectual property by Anthropic.

Beyond these cases, over 70 infringement lawsuits have been filed against AI companies by various authors, visual artists, and news outlets, including The New York Times and Getty Images. While the Bartz case set a precedent for pirating books, the broader legal landscape for mass scraping in AI training remains uncertain.

The Authors Guild is actively pursuing other lawsuits, including one against OpenAI and Microsoft, as part of a "multi-pronged approach." Their goal is to clarify legal requirements for AI companies to license the books they use.

The Guild is also collaborating with Congress to establish national legislation that mandates licensing for AI training data. This initiative aims to ensure authors and publishers are compensated and can implement filters to control how their works appear in AI outputs.

For authors like Wolff, this collective support is crucial for protecting the next generation of writers. He expresses concern for young authors' ability to sustain a career in the face of these complex technological challenges without proper compensation and attribution.
